overview.title: Broadcast maximum, and the tensor (dot) product of two vectors
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations
overview.main_topic: A final broadcasting example with np.maximum on a rank-4 and a rank-2 tensor, then the introduction of the tensor product (matmul / dot product), starting with the product of two vectors.
overview.central_idea: The tensor product (`np.matmul`, `keras.ops.matmul`, or `@`) is the most useful tensor operation; for two vectors of equal length it is the sum of element-wise products and returns a scalar.
overview.importance: The product `matmul(input, W)` is the heart of every `Dense` layer (p.52–53). This page defines it from first principles, and the vector product introduced here is the building block from which matrix–vector and matrix–matrix products are assembled on p.57.
learning_objectives: Apply the broadcasting rule to predict that np.maximum of shapes (64, 3, 32, 10) and (32, 10) yields (64, 3, 32, 10).
Name the three ways to write a tensor product in code: np.matmul, keras.ops.matmul, and the @ operator.
Recognise the dot notation z = x • y and relate it to matmul.
Trace naive_vector_product and state why its result is a scalar.
State the compatibility condition for the product of two vectors (same number of elements).
prerequisites: Vectors and matrices as rank-1 and rank-2 tensors (p.46)
The Dense layer formula output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b) (p.52)

summary:
The page opens by closing the broadcasting subsection with one more example: `np.maximum(x, y)` where `x` has shape `(64, 3, 32, 10)` and `y` has shape `(32, 10)`. Because `y`'s shape matches the two trailing axes of `x`, the rule from p.55 applies — `y` is virtually repeated over the leading axes `(64, 3)` — and the output `z` has the same shape as `x`, `(64, 3, 32, 10)`. This shows that broadcasting is not limited to addition: any element-wise two-tensor operation, such as `maximum`, benefits from it.

Subsection **2.3.3 Tensor product** then begins. The tensor product — also called the *dot product* or *matmul* (short for matrix multiplication) — is described as one of the most common and most useful tensor operations. In NumPy it is `np.matmul`, in Keras `keras.ops.matmul`, and in Python the shorthand is the `@` operator: for two random vectors of shape `(32,)`, `z = np.matmul(x, y)` and `z = x @ y` are equivalent. In mathematical notation the operation is written with a dot, `z = x • y`, which is where the name "dot product" comes from.

To explain what `matmul` actually computes, the authors start with the simplest case — two vectors — and give `naive_vector_product(x, y)`. It asserts that both inputs are rank 1 and have the same length, initialises `z = 0.0`, then loops over `i`, accumulating `x[i] * y[i]`. The closing paragraph draws the two lessons from the code: the product of two vectors is a **scalar**, and only vectors with the **same number of elements** are compatible. The next page (p.57) builds matrix–vector and matrix–matrix products on top of this vector product.

concepts.name: Tensor product (dot product, matmul)
concepts.definition: The operation that multiplies two tensors by summing products along a shared axis. For two vectors of the same length it is the sum of element-wise products, a scalar.
concepts.intuition: Lay the two vectors side by side, multiply matching entries, and add everything up — a single number that measures how much the two vectors 'agree'.
concepts.technical: In code: `np.matmul(x, y)`, `keras.ops.matmul(x, y)` or `x @ y`. For vectors: $z = \sum_i x_i y_i$. Requires `x.shape[0] == y.shape[0]`. Generalises to matrix–vector and matrix–matrix products (p.57).
concepts.significance: It is the `matmul(input, W)` inside every Dense layer and, more broadly, the operation that mixes information across features.
concepts.misconception: That `x @ y` for vectors is the same as `x * y`. `x * y` is element-wise and returns a vector; `x @ y` sums those products and returns a scalar.

concepts.name: Broadcasting (with element-wise maximum)
concepts.definition: The virtual expansion of a smaller tensor to the shape of a larger one so that an element-wise operation can be applied; it works for any element-wise binary operation, not only addition.
concepts.intuition: The same `(32, 10)` matrix `y` is held up against each of the 192 `(32, 10)` slices of `x`.
concepts.technical: `(64, 3, 32, 10)` vs `(32, 10)`: trailing axes match, broadcast over axes 0 and 1. `z[a, b, i, j] = max(x[a, b, i, j], y[i, j])`; `z.shape == x.shape`.
concepts.significance: Shows that the p.55 rule applies to a rank-2 'small' tensor and to non-arithmetic operations like maximum.
concepts.misconception: That broadcasting only works when the small tensor is a vector. Any shape that matches the trailing axes works.

concepts.name: Element-wise operation
concepts.definition: An operation applied independently to each entry (or pair of corresponding entries) of tensors; output shape equals input shape.
concepts.intuition: Same tiny computation at every position, no mixing between positions.
concepts.technical: `np.maximum` is element-wise; combined with broadcasting it handles differently shaped operands. Contrast with the tensor product, which contracts an axis.
concepts.significance: Separating shape-preserving (element-wise) from shape-changing (product) operations is the key skill for reading shapes.
concepts.example: `np.maximum(x, y)` with the shapes on this page.
concepts.misconception: That `np.maximum` and `np.max` are the same. `np.max` reduces an array to its largest value; `np.maximum` compares two arrays entry by entry.

code.title: Element-wise maximum of differently shaped tensors via broadcasting
code.original_code:
import numpy as np
x = np.random.random((64, 3, 32, 10))
y = np.random.random((32, 10))
z = np.maximum(x, y)
code.what_it_does: Creates a rank-4 tensor x of shape (64, 3, 32, 10) and a rank-2 tensor y of shape (32, 10), then computes their element-wise maximum; y is broadcast over the two leading axes of x and z has shape (64, 3, 32, 10).

line_explanations.explanation: Callout: 'x is a random tensor with shape (64, 3, 32, 10)' — 64 × 3 × 32 × 10 = 61,440 values.
Callout: 'y is a random tensor with shape (32, 10)' — matches the last two axes of x.
Callout: 'The output z has shape (64, 3, 32, 10) like x'. np.maximum compares entry by entry; the broadcasting rule from p.55 supplies the missing leading axes of y.

code.algorithm: Virtual repetition of y across axes 0 and 1, then element-wise max; no copy of y is made.
code.theory_link: Formula m2; the shape rule (a, b, … n, … m) vs (n, … m) with a = 64, b = 3 and trailing (32, 10).

parameters.role: Shape of the smaller tensor; must equal the trailing axes of x.

pitfalls: np.maximum (two-argument, element-wise) is different from np.max (reduction).
A y of shape (64, 3) would NOT broadcast here, because broadcasting aligns trailing axes, not leading ones.

code.title: naive_vector_product — the dot product of two vectors from scratch
code.original_code:
def naive_vector_product(x, y):
    assert len(x.shape) == 1
    assert len(y.shape) == 1
    assert x.shape[0] == y.shape[0]
    z = 0.0
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        z += x[i] * y[i]
    return z
code.what_it_does: Computes the dot product of two equal-length vectors by accumulating the products of corresponding entries into a running scalar sum.

line_explanations.explanation: Both inputs must be rank 1 — callout: 'x and y are NumPy vectors'.
They must have the same number of elements; this is the compatibility condition stated in the closing paragraph.
Initialise the accumulator as a float scalar — the result has rank 0.
Loop over every index i and add the product x[i] * y[i] to z.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: x, y of shape (n,). Output: a Python float equal to sum_i x[i] * y[i].
code.theory_link: Implements m1 exactly; reused on p.57 inside naive_matrix_vector_product to compute each output coefficient.

parameters.role: Second vector, same length as x.

deeper.title: One Dense unit = one dot product
deeper.body: Take a single sample `x` of shape `(784,)` and a single unit of a Dense layer with weight column `w` of shape `(784,)` and bias `b`. The unit's pre-activation is exactly `x @ w + b` — the vector product of this page plus a scalar. A layer with 10 units does 10 such dot products per sample, and `matmul(input, W)` on a batch (p.52) does them for all samples and all units at once. So the humble loop in `naive_vector_product` is, conceptually, the computation every neuron performs. (The authors imply this link by introducing the product immediately after the Dense layer formula on p.52–53.)

deeper.title: Element-wise versus contracting: watching the shapes
deeper.body:
Beyond the book: the two operation families on this page behave oppositely with respect to shape.

| operation | inputs | output | what happens to the shared axis |
|---|---|---|---|
| `np.maximum(x, y)` | (64, 3, 32, 10), (32, 10) | (64, 3, 32, 10) | kept (element-wise) |
| `x @ y` | (32,), (32,) | () | summed away (contracted) |

Element-wise ops never change rank; a product removes the shared axis. Keeping this distinction in mind makes p.57's rule — result shape `(x.shape[0], y.shape[1])` — obvious: the inner axes are contracted, the outer ones remain.

deeper.title: Why np.maximum and relu are the same idea
deeper.body:
1. p.53 defines `relu(x)` as `max(x, 0)`.
2. In NumPy that is `np.maximum(x, 0.)` — a two-argument element-wise maximum, exactly the function used on this page.
3. The scalar `0.` has shape `()`, which trivially matches the trailing axes of any shape, so it is broadcast to every element.
4. Therefore the `np.maximum(x, y)` example is the general form of which relu is the simplest instance: broadcast the small operand, compare element by element. (Steps 2–4 are my connection, not stated on the page.)

deeper.title: A shopping receipt
deeper.body: A dot product is a receipt total: `x` is the list of quantities bought and `y` the list of unit prices. Multiply each quantity by its price and add the lines — one number, the total. The two lists must have the same length (one price per item), which is the `x.shape[0] == y.shape[0]` assert, and the answer is a scalar, not a list.

questions.question: x has shape (64, 3, 32, 10) and y has shape (32, 10). What is the shape of np.maximum(x, y)?
questions.explanation: y matches the trailing axes of x, so it is broadcast over the leading (64, 3) axes and the output takes x's shape, as the callout says. (32, 10) and (64, 3) are partial shapes; no error occurs because the trailing axes agree.

questions.question: Give the three ways shown on this page to compute a tensor product in code.
questions.answer: np.matmul(x, y) in NumPy, keras.ops.matmul(x, y) in Keras, and the shorthand x @ y.
questions.explanation: The page names np.matmul and keras.ops.matmul and shows that z = x @ y is equivalent to z = np.matmul(x, y).

questions.question: Using naive_vector_product, compute the product of x = [1, 2, 3] and y = [4, 5, 6].
questions.explanation: z = 1·4 + 2·5 + 3·6 = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32. The loop accumulates each x[i]*y[i] into z starting from 0.0.

questions.question: Which statement about the product of two vectors is correct according to the page?
options: It returns a vector of the same length as the inputs
It returns a scalar and requires both vectors to have the same number of elements
It returns a matrix of shape (n, n)
It works for vectors of any two lengths
questions.answer: It returns a scalar and requires both vectors to have the same number of elements
questions.explanation: The closing paragraph states both facts. A same-length vector would be the element-wise product x * y; an (n, n) matrix would be an outer product, not discussed here; different lengths fail the assert x.shape[0] == y.shape[0].

questions.question: Why does the page call the operation 'dot product'?
questions.answer: Because in mathematical notation it is written with a dot: z = x • y.
questions.explanation: The page says 'you'd note the operation with a dot (•) (hence the name "dot product")'. The code names matmul and tensor product refer to the same operation.

questions.question: Contrast how np.maximum and the vector product treat the shapes of their inputs.
questions.answer: np.maximum is element-wise: the output keeps the (larger) input shape and broadcasting fills in missing axes. The vector product contracts the shared axis: two (32,) vectors become a single scalar.
questions.explanation: Element-wise operations never change rank, while the tensor product sums over an axis and removes it — the key difference between the two halves of this page.

questions.question: Without looking, write naive_vector_product from memory, including its three asserts. Then explain which assert encodes the 'same number of elements' rule.
questions.answer: Two rank-1 asserts (len(x.shape) == 1, len(y.shape) == 1), then assert x.shape[0] == y.shape[0] — this third one is the same-length rule; z = 0.0; loop over i accumulating x[i] * y[i]; return z.
